newsitem.title: USA: Virgin Air wants US domestic flights.
newsitem.headline: Virgin Air wants US domestic flights.

text.p: Virgin Group's Virgin Atlantic Airways said on Wednesday it would be interested in starting a low-cost domestic U.S. service if U.S. law were changed to permit foreigners to compete in the market.

Virgin chairman Richard Branson told the International Aviation Club he had been asked by people he did not name to open an economy U.S. service, similar to Southwest Airlines Co but told them U.S. law now prohibited it.
He said, however, that a true "open skies" U.S.-British aviation agreement would allow U.S. and British citizens to compete in the aviation markets between or within each country.
Branson said he had been asked to expand his low-cost Virgin Express airline, now operating in Europe, to cover cities in America not now served by Southwest Airlines.
Asked about expansion in France, he said Virgin Express was interested in buying some landing slots or other assets of troubled French airline Air Liberte, but he did not elaborate.
Branson noted that France was a slot-restricted country and access to slots was necessary for airline expansion.

Branson, whose Virgin Atlantic Airways routes include the U.S.-British market, continued his campaign against the proposed transatlantic alliance of American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, and British Airways Plc.
"If this alliance were allowed to go ahead," he said, "it would be like the merger of Coke and Pepsi, of Nike and Reebok, of General Motors and Ford."
He said competition would lessen and prices would rise.

U.S. officials have said the alliance would not be approved until the completion of a U.S.-British free-market "open skies" air accord. But U.S. officials broke off talks in August, saying British offers fell short of what was needed to reach an agreement.
Branson said, however, the "open skies" accord the United States sees as a model lacked several points, including one to liberalize restrictions on foreign ownership and control.
"A true open skies," he said, "should enable U.S. and United Kingdom citizens to compete in any part of the commercial aviation market between or within each country."
